To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in 27% of hypertensives who are not PA, ACTH drives inappropriate aldosterone secretion.
in unselected hypertensivies, 29% show inappropriate aldosterone secretion, as defined by the FDST, and that 27% of these are extremely responsive to ACTH.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the potential role(s) of the ACTH/aldosterone/cortisol axis in the genesis of PA.
the role of ACTH in aldosterone secretion, and the genesis and pathophysiology of PA.
the physiological and pathophysiological role of ACTH as a secretagogue of aldosterone.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ACTH is the most likely candidate to explain the genesis of PA.
the role of ACTH as a major aldosterone secretagogue is not fully understood, but that it may be a significant contributor to aldosterone excess in some patients with hypertension.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ACTH, in addition to angiotensins, is a potent acute aldosterone secretagoue.
ACTH, as well as being a major acute secretagogue for aldosterone, has the potential to be a chronic one, and that its effects on aldosterone may not be confined to the adrenal gland.
the ACTH-driven aldosterone response is not part of a normal feedback loop, but is a homeostasis mechanism, which is curtailed by the action of cortisol, which is itself a product of ACTH.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ACTH may play a major role in the genesis of inappropriate aldosterone secretion.
ACTH, as an acute aldosteronogenic stimulus, has a role in the genesis of PA.
the role of ACTH in driving inappropriate aldosteronism is a potential mechanism for the pathogenesis of PA.
